reviewed_by: Claude Opus 5 blind reviewer, area cluster re-review after G3 table gating, 2026-08-13

samples_reviewed.question_text: Daniel wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 3 m long and 4 m wide with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?
Kuya Bien wants to cover a square garden measuring 5 cm on each side with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?
A rectangle has an area of 15 sq cm and a length of 5 cm. What is its width?
A rectangle has an area of 8 sq m and a length of 4 m. What is its width?
Ate Cara wants to cover a square garden measuring 3 cm on each side with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?
A rectangle has an area of 21 sq m and a length of 3 m. What is its width?
A rectangle has an area of 30 sq m and a width of 5 m. What is its length?
A rectangle has an area of 28 sq cm and a width of 4 cm. What is its length?
A rectangle has an area of 24 sq m and a width of 3 m. What is its length?
A rectangle has an area of 18 sq m and a width of 3 m. What is its length?
Pia wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 5 cm long and 2 cm wide with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?
A rectangle has an area of 24 sq cm and a width of 4 cm. What is its length?
Yna wants to cover a square garden measuring 5 cm on each side with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?
Kris wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 8 m long and 5 m wide with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?

competency_fulfillment.rationale: The samples put the area inside a problem instead of asking for it outright. Seed 42 'Daniel wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 3 m long and 4 m wide with square tiles. How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?' makes the pupil recognise a covering situation as an area question, while seed 44 'A rectangle has an area of 15 sq cm and a length of 5 cm. What is its width?' supplies the area and requires the inverse step 15 divided by 5. Both kinds are problem solving that involves an area rather than the bare computation of one.

comprehensive_coverage.rationale: Both shapes named in the sentence get their own problems: squares at seed 43 'Kuya Bien wants to cover a square garden measuring 5 cm on each side with square tiles' (25) and seed 46 (3 on each side, 9), rectangles at seed 604 'Kris wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 8 m long and 5 m wide' (40) and throughout the inverse family. The inverse case is covered in both directions too, seed 45 withholding the width with 'a length of 4 m. What is its width?' and seed 500 withholding the length with 'a width of 5 m. What is its length?', and both cm and m appear on each side of that split.

cognitive_capacity.rationale: The tiling problems never say how large a tile is, so the closing question at seed 42, 'How many tiles are needed to cover it completely?', is determinate only if the pupil silently assumes a one-unit square tile, an assumption the stem gives an eight-year-old no way to make. Three of the six word problems then set the situation at an implausible size, seed 601 'Pia wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 5 cm long and 2 cm wide with square tiles', seed 46 'Ate Cara wants to cover a square garden measuring 3 cm on each side', and seed 603 'Yna wants to cover a square garden measuring 5 cm on each side with square tiles'. Seeds 42 and 604 show the same frame reading naturally in metres, so the centimetre gardens are a context slip that adds confusion rather than difficulty.

variant_comprehensiveness.rationale: Three structurally distinct problems appear rather than one template renumbered: rectangle tiling at seed 42 (3 m by 4 m), square tiling at seed 603 'Yna wants to cover a square garden measuring 5 cm on each side with square tiles', and the inverse where an area is given and a side is missing at seed 502 'A rectangle has an area of 24 sq m and a width of 3 m. What is its length?'. The inverse family itself splits between asking for the width (seeds 44, 45, 50) and asking for the length (seeds 500, 501, 502, 600, 602), and the word problems carry six different actors, Daniel, Kuya Bien, Ate Cara, Pia, Yna and Kris, so the contexts are not a single unnamed figure repeated.

competency_alignment.rationale: No sample drops into plain area computation. Every item either wraps the area in a situation to be reasoned out, as at seed 604 'Kris wants to cover a rectangular garden that is 8 m long and 5 m wide with square tiles', or consumes an area already given, as at seed 501 'A rectangle has an area of 28 sq cm and a width of 4 cm. What is its length?'. The keyed answers are tile counts and missing side lengths, never a number of square units, so none of these fourteen samples duplicates the neighbouring direct area calculation competency.

scale_appropriateness.rationale: Every inverse item is an exact division sitting inside the 3, 4 and 5 times tables: seed 44 15 divided by 5 is 3, seed 45 8 divided by 4 is 2, seed 50 'A rectangle has an area of 21 sq m and a length of 3 m' 21 divided by 3 is 7, seed 500 30 divided by 5 is 6, seed 501 28 divided by 4 is 7, seed 502 24 divided by 3 is 8, seed 600 18 divided by 3 is 6, seed 602 24 divided by 4 is 6. The largest dividend is 30, every quotient is a single digit and none leaves a remainder, so nothing calls for long division. The forward items match, running from seed 601 at 5 by 2 up to seed 604 at 8 by 5 giving 40, all within Grade 3 Quarter 1 table facts.
